doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The list exercise and why not to have a safety net
summary: He has students list everything they could do in music, the skills each needs and how to practice them; he argues against falling back on teaching.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: A little sharp is better, or it would really be a downer. There’s that, then the other things, I’ll go through a week of what I do. And I’ll say okay, now I want you to write down all the things you could do as a musician. Shows, club dates, weddings, this, that, boom, boom, boom. Make that list. Then draw a line, and write on the other side the specific skills you will need to do those specific things. What will you need to be a club date musician? Do you have to learn tunes? Do you have to learn “Feelings?” Do you need to be just more attentive as you listen to the radio so you can sing that new song “And I Will Always Love You” Whitney Houston you know? Do you need to know the song you were singing just a few minutes ago. You know what I always confuse that song with, “Get by with a little help from my friends” [scats]. Remember the commercial, “Come to a Girls’ Club and see/ come to a Girls club and be — You guys don’t remember that.
Wow. I don’t remember that one.
It’s a Girls’ Club, well anyway.
Well maybe you played on it.

Maybe I did. I hope I’m getting paid for it. What do you need to be a Broadway musician? Okay? And then you write next to it what skills you need. A studio musician. What do you need to be a soloist in a jazz club? What do you need to be a classical soloist? Sometimes I’ll get a call to play with a concert band, to play just a classical oriented program, light classics. Play “Flight of the Bumblebee” or “Virgin dela Macarena” or something, some Rafael Mendez stuff. What are the skills? What do you need to do? And then draw another line, okay, how am I going to go about achieving those things. What kind of practice schedule am I going to have to set up to make these things happen for myself? And ultimately I always tell people, find out the thing you ultimately want to do. But just have these — whereas as the people used to say get a teaching degree so you’ll have something to fall back on. And if you’re finding finally like I did at that, you didn’t want to fall back on that. I don’t want to fall back on © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
something, I want to fall into something, and what I want to fall into is the things I want to do. I want to have the trumpet mouthpiece up to my lips, because I love that.
Do you think if people set themselves for that safety net, that that’s where they’re going to end up going?

Well I didn’t want to say that, but I absolutely do. So I think if ultimately if you don’t want to teach on that kind of level — I want to teach, I definitely want to teach, I love it. But I don’t want to teach in that setting. I had so many friends graduate from school and now they’re conducting elementary school bands, which is great and I talk to elementary school kids all the time, but that’s just not my place and I know for many of my friends it’s not either, but they fell back onto something, because that’s all they knew what to fall back on. I wanted to make sure I didn’t have anything to fall — I had to fall into either playing this trumpet or not doing anything, I don’t know what else I would have done but you know it’s always like I tell people, if you can think of anything else besides music that you’d like to do, then do that. Because this is going to take every ounce of sweat that you can muster up. It’s really a hard profession, but the rewards that you get from it are so immense that if you want to do it, just do it one thousand percent.
